# Characters and strings


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

A character is an [atom](terms.qmd#term-atom), like a number, written in
single quotes. A string is a vector of any number of characters, even
one or none, written in double quotes. `''` also gives the empty string:

``` bpl
ρ'a'               ⍝ ⍬ₓ
ρ"a"               ⍝ [1]ₓ
ρ"abc"             ⍝ [3]ₓ
ρ''                ⍝ [0]ₓ
```

## Quotes inside text

The character literal for a single quote is `'''`. A string can contain
an unescaped single quote. To put a double quote inside a string, write
it twice:

``` bpl
•ucs '''           ⍝ 39ₓ
≢"can't"           ⍝ 5ₓ
≢"say ""hi"""      ⍝ 8ₓ
```

## Text across lines

A string can span lines. Every line ending inside it becomes one
newline, and its indentation stays as written. The REPL waits for the
closing quote.

``` bpl
poem←"Roses are red,
  violets are blue"
≢poem
poem
```

    33ₓ

    "Roses are red,
      violets are blue"

## Strands of text

Literals separated by spaces form one vector, called a
[strand](terms.qmd#term-strand), whether they are characters or strings:

``` bpl
'a' 'b' 'c'        ⍝ "abc"
≢"one" "three"     ⍝ 2ₓ
≢¨"one" "three"    ⍝ [3 5]ₓ
```

Keys are written as a vector of strings, as in `"x" "y":1 2`. [Axis
keys](keyed.ipynb) covers keyed arrays.

## How text is displayed

On its own, a string is displayed as plain text and a character matrix
as lines of text. Inside a larger array, strings keep their double
quotes and characters their single quotes. In the REPL:

``` text
      "abc"
abc
      2 3ρ"abcdef"
abc
def
      ⊂"ab"
⊂"ab"
      "abc",⊂"de"
'a' 'b' 'c' "de"
```

## Working with text

Functions that work on vectors work on strings too, such as `⌽`:

``` bpl
⌽"abc"
```

    "cba"

`=` compares two strings one character at a time. `≡` compares them as a
whole:

``` bpl
"abc"="abd"
"abc"≡"abd"
```

    $t $t $f

    $f

`ι` finds the first position in the left string of each character in the
right string. For a character not in the left string, `ι` gives the
length of the left string:

``` bpl
"abc"ι"cz"
```

    [2 3]ₓ

Find `⍷` marks each position where a pattern starts:

``` bpl
"an"⍷"banana"
```

    $f $t $f $t $f $f

`<` sorts characters by code point:

``` bpl
<"bca"
```

    "abc"

Adding a whole number to a character moves it along the Unicode code
points. Subtracting one character from another gives the distance
between their code points:

``` bpl
'a'+3
'a'+ι3ₓ
'd'-'a'
```

    'd'

    "abc"

    3ₓ

The order comparisons, such as `<`, compare characters by code point. A
number is less than any character.

[System functions](system-functions.qmd) cover the rest of text
handling. `•ucs` converts between characters and code points:

``` bpl
•ucs "ABC"
```

    [65 66 67]ₓ

`•c` changes case:

``` bpl
•c "Hello"
```

    "hello"

`$a` holds the uppercase alphabet, and `$d` holds the digits. `∊` tests
which characters are in `$d`:

``` bpl
"a2b"∊$d
```

    $f $t $f

`⍕` formats any value as text:

``` bpl
"Total: ",⍕+/1.5 2
```

    "Total: 3.5"

[Regular expressions](regex.ipynb) covers matching patterns in text with
`•r`.
